title: The third meal
hookLine: a slow meal at dusk, with quiet songs as the day fades

lines: THE LAST HOUR OF A VACATION.
cards: The last hour of a good vacation. The bags are packed. The light is going gold.
Part of you is already back at work, answering email in your head. Part of you wants to hold on to every last minute. Late on Saturday afternoon, as the sun goes down, Shabbat reaches that hour.
And instead of rushing to the end, the custom is to sit down to eat. Again. A small meal, in fading light, with songs that get slower and quieter as the room gets darker.
Today: seudah shlishit, the third meal.

teach.b: Seudah means meal and shlishit means third. Friday night dinner is the first Shabbat meal, Saturday lunch the second, and this is the third. Why a third?

When Moses told the people about the first Shabbat, he said, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "Eat that to-day; for to-day is a sabbath unto the LORD; to-day ye shall not find it in the field."
The rabbis counted: today, today, today. Three times, so three meals. The third doesn't have to be big.
Some people have challah and a little fish or salad. In some communities it happens in the synagogue between the afternoon and evening prayers, at long tables, with the lights low or off.
And it's the songs people remember.
Slow, longing songs. Some sing the Twenty-third Psalm, the LORD is my shepherd. Others sing Yedid Nefesh, beloved of the soul, a love poem to God by Eleazar Azikri, a Kabbalist of Safed.

Hasidic tradition calls this hour a time of special closeness, the favor of favors, when the day's holiness is at its fullest just before it leaves. Often there's no talking between the songs. People hum.
Someone starts a tune, and it goes around the table again and again.
The whole meal says: we know it's ending, and we're not going to hurry it along. You stay at the table until you really can't see.

how: Late on Saturday afternoon, Jews who keep the custom eat a small third meal, at home or in synagogue between the afternoon and evening prayers, often in dim light with slow songs such as Yedid Nefesh and Psalm 23.

the big festive lunch on Saturday at midday

three meals come from 'today' said three times
"eat that to-day; for to-day is a sabbath... to-day ye shall not find it."
the third meal is eaten in bright light with loud songs
it's at dusk, often with lights low, and the songs are slow and quiet.

games.q: it's late Saturday afternoon. Shabbat is nearly over. you've already had two big meals. what does the custom say to do now?
o: skip ahead and start the week early.
sit down for a small, slow third meal.
games.why: they sit down again, at home or in synagogue, and sing slow songs as the light fades, refusing to hurry the ending.

practice: Picture this evening as the light starts to fade: something simple on a plate, no screen, maybe with someone, maybe alone. Take the first bite slowly, notice the light changing on the wall, and hum something if you like.
When the food's gone, stay a minute more, until it's really dark.

wordCard.voice: Seudah shlishit. The third meal: a small, slow meal at dusk on Shabbat, with quiet songs as the day fades.

orig.note: Hebrew: the third meal. Hasidim also call it raava d'raavin, the favor of favors, in Aramaic.

carryVoice: Your line: don't rush the ending. Even the close of Shabbat gets a meal of its own. See you tomorrow.
